newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina moves on labor reform despite strike.
newsitem.headline: Argentina moves on labor reform despite strike.

text.p: The Argentine government, undaunted by a general strike just a day away, said on Wednesday it will send to Congress next week a bill making labour laws more flexible to help companies lower their costs.
"They can stage one or 1,000 strikes but our economic plan will not be changed or negotiated," a defiant President Carlos Menem said.

Other senior officials sought to persuade unions to call off a 36-hour walkout set for Thursday to protest austerity measures and labour reforms and express anger at 17.1 percent unemployment. But the CGT, the largest labour federation, which is organising the protest and has negotiated the contracts for most of Argentina's unionized workers, would not back down.
Two opinion polls published on Wednesday indicated that betweeen 54 and 69 percent of Argentines support the strike. But only 30 percent in one survey said they would walk out.

The reforms include loosening restrictions on working hours and holidays, allowing for wages to vary depending on economic conditions and for overtime to be payable in days off in lieu of cash, and creating unemployment insurance schemes funded by employers. They also allow companies to negotiate contracts directly with their workers in place of separate industries striking collective wage deals with trade unions.

Authorities argue the reforms are needed to lower employer costs and give firms flexibility to change working conditions to suit the economic climate, making them more competitive. The government predicts that employers, with lower costs, will hire workers again and help slash the jobless rate to single digit levels by the end of the decade.

"Many of the collective agreements negotiated by the CGT make fast and efficient responses to (economic) change difficult, costly, slow or impossible," reads a draft for the government's labour bill released late on Tuesday.

The ruling Peronist Party's majority in Congress has shown only lukewarm support at best for the reforms, with Jorge Matzkin, leader in the lower house, telling Reuters recently he had no evidence previous reforms created jobs.
But Labour Minister Armando Caro Figueroa reiterated a government threat to impose the reforms by decree by the end of the year if Congress refuses to approve them.
Congress is also debating several austerity measures, including an increase in fuel taxes, to narrow a widening budget deficit.
